summary:
Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in the Cayman Islands in 2001 by an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature declined to act, and the reform left an unequal age of consent in its wake.

London–local friction over the scope of protections is documented from 2009, when the United Kingdom's Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the draft Cayman Islands constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission deplorable and warning that the drafting could leave the territory's courts affording less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the draft's list of discrimination grounds was open-ended.

The judiciary outran the legislature on relationship status. In March 2019 Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the prohibition on same-sex marriage; the Court of Appeal reversed that ruling in August 2019, so no same-sex marriages can be performed locally. In December 2020 the immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had married in Ireland, with the Court of Appeal holding that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. The practical position for a visitor is therefore recognition of an existing foreign marriage for immigration effects, without any locally conferred marital status.

Public visibility carries official backing. The territory's first Pride parade, held on 7 August 2021 and organised by the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation, drew around 600 participants including the premier, the governor, ministers and members of the Legislative Assembly. Participants were asked by organisers to refrain from excessive displays of affection, a condition reflecting sensitivities about public space rather than a legal prohibition.
tangentialFactors:
The Cayman Islands presents a pattern in which official tolerance and judicial protection run ahead of the legislature. Public events enjoy visible participation by the territory's most senior officeholders, while the statutory position on marriage remains restrictive and the age of consent has not been equalised.

The recognition ruling establishes a distinction that shapes visitor expectations: a valid foreign marriage can be given legal effect in immigration matters even though the same union cannot be contracted locally. Refusing that effect was held to be unequal treatment on sexual-orientation grounds.

The 2009 exchange with the United Kingdom's Foreign Affairs Committee shows that disputes over how far anti-discrimination protection extends have been conducted between London and the territory's own framers, with the local argument resting on the open-ended character of the listed discrimination grounds.
localsOnly:
Residents cannot marry a same-sex partner locally, since the March 2019 Grand Court ruling that struck down the marriage prohibition was overturned on appeal in August 2019. A resident who marries abroad may find that marriage recognised for Cayman Islands immigration purposes following the December 2020 Court of Appeal decision, but that recognition does not by itself confer marital status within the territory.

The unequal age of consent introduced alongside the 2001 decriminalisation remains the operative statutory position on the evidence available, and continues to expose residents to differential treatment under the criminal law.

Officials participate openly in LGBTQ community events: the premier, the governor, ministers and Legislative Assembly members joined the roughly 600 attendees at the first Pride parade on 7 August 2021. Organisers' request that participants avoid excessive displays of affection was a condition set by the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation for the public-space event.

The constitutional text is defended on the basis that its list of discrimination grounds is open-ended rather than exhaustive, an argument the Foreign and Commonwealth Office advanced against the Foreign Affairs Committee's criticism in 2009.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the unequal age of consent identified after the 2001 decriminalisation has since been amended by the Legislative Assembly is unresolved in the available sources; no later legislative text is provided.

The scope of the December 2020 recognition beyond immigration effects is unresolved. Whether a foreign same-sex marriage is given general legal effect in the Cayman Islands, for purposes such as property, succession or next-of-kin status, is not sourced here.

No source in the inventory addresses whether the territory has enacted a civil partnership, domestic partnership or equivalent status scheme, or whether any such bill is pending.

Nothing in the inventory covers hate-crime provisions, their wording or their enforcement, or recorded incidents of violence against trans people in the Cayman Islands. Those questions remain unsourced rather than answered negatively.

Whether the Court of Appeal's equality reasoning in the recognition case has been applied to other areas of law, and whether any further appeal or legislative response followed, is not established by the available material.
